You're building the sellable foundation for 5 games on Nxeon (VPS/game-hosting platform, Next.js/Prisma/Postgres, staging tree at /opt/nxeon-staging — work ONLY in staging, never /opt/nxeon prod. Do NOT run `npm run build`; verify with `npx tsc --noEmit` only).

Context: 5 games were data-scaffolded today at the lib layer only: Dragonwilds, Sunkenland, Abiotic Factor (slug `abioticfactor`), Core Keeper, Icarus — defined in `lib/games.ts` with explicit comments "SCAFFOLD ONLY 2026-08-31, NOT yet orderable — no GamePlan/OsTemplate seeded" and "art not yet produced" (art is being handled by a parallel task, not your job). The owner wants these actually sellable now — real pricing tiers, real provisioning.

Your job:
1. Investigate the existing pattern: find how an already-live, similar game (pick 2-3 comparable Steam-dedicated-server survival/co-op games already sellable today, e.g. Valheim, Palworld, ARK, Conan Exiles, or Enshrouded — check `lib/games.ts` for the full existing roster) is set up end-to-end: its `GamePlan` pricing tier rows (check `prisma/seed-wave1-games.ts`, `prisma/seed-wave2-games.ts`, `prisma/seed-gameplans.ts`, or wherever `GamePlan` seeding actually lives — grep for `GamePlan` across `prisma/`), its `OsTemplate` row (the provisioning template — likely references a SteamCMD app ID and a launch/install script), and whatever `worker/` code actually installs+starts the dedicated server for it (grep `worker/` for that game's family key to find the install/start script — likely SteamCMD-based with a specific Steam App ID and launch command per game).
2. For each of the 5 new games, find its real Steam dedicated-server App ID and correct launch parameters/config file format (research via WebSearch/WebFetch if not already known — check SteamDB, the game's official wiki, or its Steam store page for "Dedicated Server" App ID; these are public IDs, standard practice to look up). Confirm each of the 5 genuinely has a real, official (or at minimum a broadly legitimate, standard SteamCMD-based) dedicated server — if any of the 5 turns out NOT to have real dedicated server support after all (contradicting the earlier research that qualified them), STOP for that game and report it as a blocker rather than seeding fake data.
3. For games that check out, add: (a) `GamePlan` pricing tier rows matching the existing tier/pricing pattern used by comparable games (same RAM/CPU/disk tiers and similar price points — don't invent a wildly different pricing scheme), (b) an `OsTemplate` row wired to the correct SteamCMD App ID, (c) worker-side install/start script support (following the exact pattern of the comparable existing game you studied in step 1 — reuse the existing generic SteamCMD worker machinery if one exists rather than writing bespoke code per game, unless a game genuinely needs bespoke handling, e.g. unusual config format).
4. After seeding, confirm the game now appears in the deploy wizard's game list on staging (check `app/dashboard/deploy/page.tsx`'s `GAME_FAMILIES.filter(f => withTiers.has(f))` logic mentioned in a prior investigation — your new `GamePlan` rows should make `withTiers` include these games now).
5. Do NOT touch `/opt/nxeon` (prod) — staging DB only. Do NOT enable any prod-facing purchase flow. This is staging-only foundation work for the owner to review before promoting.
6. Run `npx tsc --noEmit` and confirm clean.

Report back per-game: which games got fully seeded and are now orderable on staging (confirm via the deploy-wizard check), which (if any) hit a real blocker (no real dedicated server support, or something else) and why, exact pricing tiers you seeded (so the owner can review/adjust), and the Steam App IDs used. Keep it a clear scannable table, under 500 words.
